title: No Favoritism: The Judge Who Judges Others
summary: Paul turns to the reader who has agreed with his condemnation of the idolatrous world and tells him that in judging others he condemns himself. God judges impartially, according to truth and according to deeds, Jew and Gentile alike. Having the law, teaching it, and bearing the sign of circumcision do not protect anyone who breaks it; the true Jew is one inwardly, whose heart has been circumcised by the Spirit.
story: Chapter 1 ended with a grim portrait of a world that exchanged God's glory for idols. A devout Jewish reader of Paul's day would have nodded along, since the critique followed familiar Jewish lines, and so might a morally serious Gentile. Chapter 2 springs the trap. The one who condemns others does the same things, and God's judgment has no favorites. Paul is building toward the verdict of 3:9 and 3:19-20: Jews and Greeks alike are under sin, and no one is justified by works of the law. This chapter removes the last place a reader might stand to watch the judgment from outside.
historical:
Paul writes as a Jew who had been a Pharisee, deeply trained in the law (Philippians 3:5-6), and the confidence he describes in verses 17-20 is not a caricature. Jewish communities across the Roman world were proud, with good reason, of having God's law, of their monotheism in a world of idols, and of their calling to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6, 49:6). Many Gentiles admired Jewish ethics and attended synagogues as God-fearers. Paul's charge is not that this calling was false but that possessing it did not guarantee living it.

The question of rob temples in verse 22 has puzzled readers. Jews abhorred idols, and handling objects from pagan temples was forbidden (Deuteronomy 7:25-26). Paul may mean that some Jews profited from stolen temple goods, or he may be using the phrase more broadly for sacrilege. Josephus mentions an incident in Rome in AD 19 in which Jewish swindlers took gifts meant for the Jerusalem temple from a Roman convert, leading to an expulsion of Jews from the city. Whether Paul had any such case in mind is uncertain.
cultural:
Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17) and the chief marker of Jewish identity in the Greco-Roman world, where many Greeks and Romans found it strange or distasteful. For a Gentile man to be circumcised was to become a Jew. So Paul's claim that circumcision becomes uncircumcision for the one who breaks the law, and that an uncircumcised person who keeps the law will be counted as circumcised, cut close to the bone. He did not invent the idea of a circumcised heart. Moses called Israel to circumcise their hearts (Deuteronomy 10:16) and promised that God would do it for them (Deuteronomy 30:6), and Jeremiah pressed the same demand (Jeremiah 4:4).

The wordplay at the end of the chapter would have been clearer to readers who knew Hebrew. The name Judah, from which Jew comes, is linked in Genesis 29:35 to the Hebrew word for praise. A true Jew, Paul says, is one whose praise comes from God, not from people.
literary: Paul writes in the style of the diatribe, a teaching form in which the speaker addresses an imagined conversation partner, poses his questions, and answers them. The sudden you and O man of verses 1 and 3 are not a particular person in Rome but a figure Paul argues with. Verses 6-11 are arranged as a chiasm: God repays by deeds (A), eternal life for those who do good (B), wrath for those who do evil (C), then trouble for evildoers (C'), glory for those who do good (B'), and God shows no favoritism (A'). Verses 17-24 build a long chain of if-clauses describing the teacher's privileges, then turn into a series of piercing questions: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” The chapter ends with the contrast between letter and Spirit that Paul will develop in chapter 7.

outline.t: The one who judges condemns himself
God repays each according to deeds, without favoritism
Law, conscience, and the day of judgment
Relying on the law while breaking it

doctrines.note: God's judgment is according to truth, according to deeds, and without favoritism, and it will reach even the secrets of the heart through Christ Jesus (verse 16). Privilege and knowledge do not exempt anyone from it.
God's kindness, tolerance, and patience are meant to lead people to repentance (verse 4). Delay in judgment is not indifference; it is mercy, and presuming on it hardens the heart.
Paul says the law's requirements can be written on the heart and that true circumcision is by the Spirit. The law is not the problem; the problem is hearing it without doing it.
Gentiles without the written law still have a conscience that accuses or defends them (verse 15). Every person has some knowledge of right and wrong, and so every person is accountable.

words.note: Prosopolempsia, favoritism, literally receiving the face: judging by who a person is rather than what they have done. The idea comes from the Old Testament command that judges not show partiality (Deuteronomy 10:17). Paul applies it to God's judgment of Jew and Gentile.

Chrestotes, kindness or goodness. Paul says it is God's kindness that leads to repentance. The word appears again in 11:22 (the kindness and severity of God) and in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

Suneidesis, conscience, the inner witness that judges one's own actions. Paul says Gentile consciences bear witness alongside the law written on their hearts. Conscience is a real guide, but in Paul it can also be weak or seared, so it is not the final judge.

Peritome, circumcision. It appears six times in verses 25-29. Paul does not deny its value (3:1-2), but he insists that the outward sign without the inward reality counts for nothing before God, echoing the prophets.

christ: Paul says that God will judge people's secrets through Christ Jesus (verse 16). The one who will be the judge is the one the gospel proclaims, so the good news and the coming judgment are not opposed; the Judge is also the Savior. The chapter's picture of the heart circumcised by the Spirit points ahead to what Christ's work accomplishes, the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:33, where God writes his law on hearts. In chapter 2 Paul has not yet told us how that happens. He is closing every door but one, and the door he leaves open is Christ, described in 3:21-26.

hard.q: Does Romans 2 teach that people are saved by doing good works?
hard.a:
Verses 7, 10, and 13 speak of eternal life for those who persist in doing good and say that the doers of the law will be declared righteous. Yet in 3:20 Paul says no one will be justified by works of the law. Interpreters have offered several resolutions.

One reading, common in the Reformation tradition, takes these verses as stating the law's standard in principle: if anyone perfectly did good, they would be justified, but chapter 3 shows that no one does. A second reading holds that Paul is describing Christian believers, including Gentiles, whose lives are changed by the Spirit so that they truly fulfill the law; the Gentiles of verses 14-15 with the law written on their hearts would then be Christians, echoing Jeremiah 31. A third reading says that final judgment really is according to works for everyone, and that for believers those works are the fruit and evidence of faith, not its basis. Many interpreters combine the second and third. All agree that Paul is not contradicting his own teaching that justification comes by grace through faith, and all agree that he takes the moral life seriously: grace never makes obedience irrelevant.

questions: Paul says we condemn ourselves when we judge others for things we also do. Where are you most quick to judge?
How have you experienced God's kindness as something that leads you to change rather than something to take for granted?
What outward signs of religion can people rely on in place of a changed heart, and how would you know if you were doing that?
